sources.title: Bank barn

links.claim: The later barn largely developed from the medieval aisled barn; where walls were of stone the aisled timber frame often gave way to a single span.

sources.title: Barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The modern barn largely developed from the three aisled medieval barn, commonly known as tithe barn or monastic barn.

sources.title: Barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Whenever stone walls were applied, the aisled timber frame often gave way to single-naved buildings.

links.claim: The great aisled barns of the Middle Ages are commonly called tithe barns; many were monastic barns, and the name is often wrong.

sources.title: Barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: the three aisled medieval barn, commonly known as tithe barn or monastic barn

sources.title: Tithe barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Many were monastic barns, originally used by the monastery itself or by a monastic grange.

links.claim: A threshing barn is a barn with a central threshing floor.

sources.title: Threshing barn (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 71296)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A barn usually containing a single, central threshing floor.

links.claim: A cruck barn is a barn whose roof is carried on pairs of curved timbers (crucks), used in the Middle Ages for houses and large barns.

sources.title: Cruck barn (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 91679)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A barn in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.

sources.title: Cruck
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Crucks were chiefly used in the medieval period for structures such as houses and large tithe barns, which were entirely timber-framed.

links.claim: The bank barn, built into a slope with a threshing floor above and animals below, appears in Cumbria by the 1660s on the farms of wealthy farmers fattening Scottish drove cattle; its origins in Britain are obscure.

sources.title: Bank barn (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 71448)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A multi-purpose, two-storey barn, built on a hillside with entrances at both levels to a first floor threshing barn and ground floor animal housing.

sources.title: Bank barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The bank barn had made its first appearance in Cumbria by the 1660s on the farms of wealthy farmers

sources.title: Bank barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The origins of bank barns in the UK are obscure.

links.claim: The Dutch barn of the British Isles, for hay and straw only, often open-sided, is a relatively recent development, mostly 19th century.

sources.title: Hay barn (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 71528)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A special type of barn, lacking a threshing floor, usually with open walls, intended for the dry and well ventilated storage of hay only.

sources.title: Dutch barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the United Kingdom a structure called a Dutch barn is a relatively recent agricultural development meant specifically for hay and straw storage; most examples were built from the 19th century.

links.claim: The gin gang was added to the threshing barn to house the horse engine that drove a threshing machine inside the barn.

sources.title: Gin gang
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A gin gang, wheelhouse, roundhouse or horse-engine house is a structure built to enclose a horse engine, usually circular but sometimes square or octagonal, attached to a threshing barn.

sources.title: Threshing machine
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Some were housed in a specially constructed building, a gin gang, which would be attached to a threshing barn.

links.claim: The first oast houses were adapted barns; by the 18th century tall kilns with conical roofs had been developed for the draught, square at first, round from about 1800.

sources.title: Oast house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Early oast houses were simply adapted barns, but by the 18th century the distinctive tall buildings with conical roofs had been developed to increase the draught.

sources.title: Oast house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: At first, these were square, but around 1800 roundel kilns were developed in the belief that they were more efficient.

links.claim: Dove-keeping in England is first known from nest-holes in Norman castle keeps of the 12th century (Rochester); the free-standing dovecote follows (the earliest surely dated, 1326). The sources give the order, not the descent.

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The earliest known examples of dove-keeping occur in Norman castles of the 12th century (for example, at Rochester Castle, Kent, where nest-holes can be seen in the keep), and documentary references also begin in the 12th century.

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The earliest surviving, definitely dated free-standing dovecote in England was built in 1326 at Garway in Herefordshire.

links.claim: The Romans may have brought dovecotes to Britain (pigeon holes at Caerwent), but doves are thought not to have been commonly kept until after the Norman Conquest.

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Romans may have introduced dovecotes or columbaria to Britain since pigeon holes have been found in Roman ruins at Caerwent.

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: However, it is believed that doves were not commonly kept there until after the Norman Conquest.

views: Roman introduction: pigeon holes in the Roman ruins at Caerwent.
Norman introduction: doves not commonly kept until after the Conquest; the earliest known dove-keeping is in 12th-century Norman castles.

links.claim: The Pennine laithe house, like the longhouse, keeps family and farm building under one roof, but as a house attached to a laithe (cow-house and crop store) rather than one long range shared with the animals. No source found derives one from the other.

sources.title: Connected farm
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The laithe house confines the family and the farm building under the same roof.

sources.title: Laithe house (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 71406)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A laithe with an attached house.

sources.title: Laithe (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 71396)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A building combining a cow-house with crop storage space.
